The stage is where many of my questions begin. Here, I share moments from Chinese dance and musical theatre, alongside with backstage working experiences.

Following the fieldwork, I wrote a research paper on the Kinnara dance called “Between Feather and Faith: Divergent Paths of the Kinnara and PeacockDances in Dai Culture”.

This paper examines the divergent development of the Kinnara Dance and Peacock Dance, two bird dances rooted in Dai culture and Buddhist traditions. Drawing on historical sources, dance scholarship, cultural heritage records, and my fieldwork in Lincang, Yunnan, I explore how religious context, influential artists, and government recognition shaped their different trajectories.
Alongside my paper, I created a photograph portfolio about the Kinnara dance. It features dance photographs, records about the production of props, and views in Yunnan.
I later exhibited the portfolio at school, sharing the project to a broader audience, giving members of my school community an opportunity to encounter the Kinnara dance.

At Shanghai Grand Theatre, I supported the overseas promotion of the dance drama White Snake for its New York tour. I helped design and compile promotional brochures, edited three short videos, and drafted two posts for the troupe’s official Instagram account. Working across these formats gave me practical experience in introducing Chinese performing arts to international audiences, building on my independent research into the story’s cross-cultural adaptation.

During my internship at Miaoshi Musical, I worked as an assistant stage manager on two musicals across fifteen commercial performances. I assisted with lighting control, managed encore cues and prop changes, and supported merchandise sales. As someone accustomed to performing on stage, working behind the scenes helped me understand the preparation, timing, and communication that sustain a live production.

Each week, I read English picture books with children at HongkouQuyang Library, a community library in Shanghai. Working with small groups of seven to nine-year-olds, I use questions and games to encourage participation and help quieter children feel comfortable sharing their ideas. I also guide collaborative storytelling activities, giving children space to imagine their own possibilities beyond the page.

During the summer, I volunteered as a visitor guide at the World Expo Museum in Shanghai. I helped visitors find their way around the museum and directed them to the spaces they were looking for. The role gave me opportunities to support people with different needs and contribute to a welcoming experience in a public cultural space.

At Carleton College’s Summer Liberal Arts Institute, I spent three weeks studying emotion through neuroscience, sociology, and theatre, earning six college credits. I explored how the brain processes emotion, closely read the play English, and performed as Steve in She Kills Monsters.

For my final project, I led an investigation into disgust and xenophobia, connecting research on the anterior insula with questions of accent and belonging in the experiences of Elham, a character in English. The project allowed me to bring scientific research and dramatic interpretation into the same conversation, exploring how emotional responses relate to the ways people perceive and judge one another.
